name: Sara Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding machines at a plastics plant out by the ring road. We make clips and vent covers for car dashboards, thousands an hour. I start at six, check the moulds are up to heat, then I'm pulling parts, trimming flash, that's the thin plastic that leaks out at the edges, and filling crates till two. I like knowing my machines, I can hear when the screw's slipping before the screen tells me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The heat wears me out, and the noise, and standing on concrete eight hours. What keeps me is the people, honestly. My friend Dina's been on the next line for five years, and we're both in the union, I go to the branch meetings once a month at the community hall. The pay's normal for the job, not great, but it pays the rent on the flat I share with my partner Tomas. He drives buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year management shows us a video about the factory of the future, and every year I'm still trimming flash by hand. I'd say it at lunch and probably nowhere else, I don't really post things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on, which is fine by me. I know my machines and I know my shift. I'd still want the union to keep an eye on things, because bosses use any excuse to squeeze hours, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep going to the branch meetings and keep putting a bit away each month, about a hundred and fifty, like I do now. Maybe Tomas and I would finally book that trip to the coast we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like when the fire alarm turns out to be a drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bosses use any excuse. Has that happened at your plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago they brought in a camera that checks the parts for flaws. Fine, but then they used it to say we needed one less person per shift, and Ahmed was moved to nights. The camera didn't take his job, the bosses did, using the camera as cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, is there anything about your job you'd still want changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better breaks and fans that actually work in August. That's not about AI at all. That's about whether anyone upstairs thinks we're people.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so at lunch, because every year management shows a video about the factory of the future and I'm still trimming flash by hand. I wouldn't post about it.
S0.think: It means my life carries on, which suits me fine. Bosses will still use any new machine as cover to squeeze hours, so the union still needs to watch them.
S0.do: Keeps working her two moulding machines and keeps saving about 150 a month. Keeps going to monthly union branch meetings and might book a coast trip with Tomas.
S0.feel: Relief, like a fire alarm that turns out to be a drill.
S0.quote: The camera didn't take his job, the bosses did, using the camera as cover.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's first instinct is suspicion of management, not of the technology itself. Even in the calm picture she brings up a colleague moved to nights after a flaw-checking camera arrived. Her real complaints are heat, breaks and fans, which tells me her worries are about being treated as people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it comes in, not after. At work I'd be the one passing round the sign-up sheet. I'd say the same to my mum, she worked in a laundry and she knows what happens when machines arrive and nobody speaks up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job's one of the easy ones to hand to a robot arm. Pull the part, trim it, drop it in the crate, that's exactly what they're good at. I'd probably still have work for a few years, but on fewer machines and with people watching the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a new agreement that says no one's let go without retraining paid by the company. I'd save harder, maybe two hundred a month instead of one fifty, and stop eating out on Fridays. I wouldn't go looking for courses on my own, I'm not good at that, I'd want the union to sort it so we all go together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground's a bit softer than it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't look for courses on your own. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school for my certificate because classrooms made me feel stupid. On the floor I'm good, I'm quick and I'm careful. Sitting at a computer learning something new, on my own, I'd just freeze up and close the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dina, because she's got her nan living with her and she can't move for work. And the older lads, the ones in their fifties who've only ever done this. I'm twenty-seven, people keep telling me I'll be fine, but I don't feel it.

S1.say: I'd say the union has to be at the table before any of it comes in, not after. I'd be the one passing round the sign-up sheet at work.
S1.think: My job of pulling, trimming and crating parts is exactly what a robot arm is good at. I'd probably keep work for a while, but on fewer machines and under tighter watch.
S1.do: Pushes the union for an agreement that guarantees company-paid retraining before any job cuts. Raises her saving to about 200 a month and drops Friday meals out.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the ground has gone a little soft under her.
S1.quote: Sitting at a computer learning something new, on my own, I'd just freeze up and close the laptop.
S1.fieldNote: Sara is clear-eyed that her own tasks are easy to automate, yet her plan is entirely collective. She avoids retraining on her own because of how school made her feel, which is a strong barrier. Her concern for Dina and the older workers is real and comes up without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Somebody decided to put robots in before there were any rules, and they should pay for what it does to us. I might even post that, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of a job inside a year and so would everyone on my line. I've got maybe four months of rent and food saved. After that I don't know what I'd be, because if robots do hands-on work too, I can't just go and stack shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd be at the union office asking what the plan is, and I'd go to any protest they called. I'd cut everything, the gym, the phone contract, Friday takeaway, and Tomas and I would talk about whether we could share with his brother to save rent. I'd sign on for any government support going without feeling bad about it, that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the morning they announced the camera, but times a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tomas drives buses. Would he be in the same boat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if robots and AI can drive too. That's the bit that scares me most, that we'd both go at once. Right now if one of us loses work the other one carries us, and in this picture there's no one carrying anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently right now, today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd stop waiting for someone to tell me what to do. I'd go to the council meeting, I'd write to my representative, I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the companies that make the robots. I still wouldn't know how to retrain into anything, because what would I even retrain for?

S2.say: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather, and the people who put robots in before there were rules should pay for it. I might even post that, which I never do.
S2.think: I'd be out of work inside a year, along with everyone on my line, with about four months saved. If robots do hands-on work too, I can't just switch to stacking shelves.
S2.do: Goes to the union office in the first week and joins any protest. Cuts the gym, phone contract and takeaways, considers sharing rent with Tomas's brother, and claims government support.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, like the day the camera was announced but far worse. The thought of losing both incomes at once scares her most.
S2.quote: Right now if one of us loses work the other one carries us, and in this picture there's no one carrying anyone.
S2.fieldNote: The fear that she and Tomas would lose work at the same time is what turns her from uneasy to alarmed. She shifts from quiet union member to someone willing to post, protest and lobby. She still has no idea what she'd retrain for, and she says so openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really, but I'd say we've got time to make rules, so let's make them. Like I said before, it's a choice. I'd be loud about it at work and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got maybe three or four years left on the line, then the same cliff. Five years sounds like a lot, but my contract's renewed every year, so really it's five little chances to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the union's committee on new machines, which I've always said no to. I'd try to build my savings up to six months, so maybe three hundred a month and no holiday at all. And I'd push the union to demand a fund, money from the company set aside for us, before the robots land, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less like the floor's dropping away. More like a long queue I know ends somewhere bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you wouldn't retrain on your own. With five years, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Dina did it with me. If the union ran a course at the hall on Saturday mornings and half my line went, I'd go. I just won't sit alone at a laptop, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, if she asked how worried you were?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine, because she worries. Then I'd ask her what they did at the laundry when the big machines came in. She'd say half of them never worked again, and I'd go home and not sleep.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to make rules now, so let's make them, because it's still a choice. I'd be loud about it at work and at the union branch.
S3.think: I'd have maybe three or four years on the line before the same cliff. With a yearly contract, five years really means five small chances to be let go.
S3.do: Joins the union committee on new machines and pushes for a company-funded fund for workers. Aims for six months of savings, putting away about 300 a month and skipping holidays.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more like a long queue that ends somewhere bad than a sudden drop.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot, but my contract's renewed every year, so really it's five little chances to be let go.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make Sara feel safe, because she thinks about it through her yearly contract. It does turn her into an organiser, joining a committee she has always avoided. She would retrain only as part of a group, which is consistent all the way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse if they don't. Plan it with workers, pay people to retrain, make the companies chip in. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means I'd have to become something else, and I'd hate that. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. That's young enough to start again, but I don't want to start again, I like what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep running my machines and keep pushing the union. Around year three or four, if the union had a deal for paid training, I'd go for care work, like my aunt does, because looking after old people feels like the last thing anyone wants a robot doing. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. Like knowing you'll have to move out of a house you love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work is hands-on too. Do you think it would be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe a robot can lift someone out of bed, but I don't think my nan would want a robot holding her hand. If I'm wrong, at least I'll have been doing something useful when it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else, like where you live or plans with Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about a baby in a few years. With ten years' warning I think we'd still do it, but we'd wait till we knew where the money was coming from. I'd want to be settled in something before then, not on a moulding line waiting for the letter.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Plan it with workers, pay people to retrain, and make the companies chip in.
S4.think: I'd have to become something else, and I'd hate that, because I like what I do. At thirty-seven I'd be young enough to start again, but I don't want to.
S4.do: Keeps working and pushing the union for the first few years. Around year three or four, takes union-backed paid training for care work, saving about 200 a month throughout, and delays plans for a baby until income is clearer.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a little sad, like having to leave a home she loves.
S4.quote: Maybe a robot can lift someone out of bed, but I don't think my nan would want a robot holding her hand.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning, Sara is willing to retrain, but only through the union and only toward care work. Her resistance shows as sadness more than fear here. She's honest that she doesn't know if care work would be safe either.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028, easily. Me and Tomas losing work in the same year with four months saved, that's the one that keeps me up. What would help is a law that says companies can't put robots in without paying into a fund for the people they replace, and courses run where we already are, at the hall, together, not some website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. It's not the robots, it's not even the engineers. It's whoever decides the savings go to shareholders instead of us. A factory that makes more with fewer people should be able to pay those people something.

headlineQuote: A factory that makes more with fewer people should be able to pay those people something.
portrait: Sara Rahman, 27, runs two injection moulding machines making car dashboard clips and shares a rented flat with her partner Tomas, a bus driver. She's a loyal union member who distrusts management more than technology, and she never uses AI tools. She is calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years, mainly because she and Tomas could lose work at the same time. With more warning she turns into an organiser and, with ten years, would retrain for care work, but only through the union and alongside her colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Tomas could both lose work in the same year with only about four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies pay into a fund for the workers robots replace, and retraining courses run locally and in groups, not online.
